extracted.intended_audience: DoD health affairs staff, military hospital administrators, and productivity/healthcare analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, computing, and evaluating hospital workload/productivity measures for Department of Defense medical facilities (comparison of Composite Work Unit and proposed Health Care Unit, including weight derivation and index computation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite Work Unit limitation — does not distinguish necessary vs unnecessary occupied bed days
rubrics_metrics.description: The Composite Work Unit 'makes no distinction between a "necessary" occupied bed day and an "unnecessary" occupied bed day.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism: each unnecessary occupied bed day inflates average daily occupied bed day input and the Composite Work Unit, biasing measured productivity downward when lengths of stay fall for good clinical/policy reasons. When measuring trends, adjustments should be made to account for policy-driven reductions in length of stay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite Work Unit limitation — insensitive to changes in length of stay and turnover
rubrics_metrics.description: The Composite Work Unit does not take rapid patient turnover or changes in average length of stay into consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: hospitals emphasizing short lengths of stay must be evaluated from the standpoint of patient turnover rather than raw Composite Work Units; otherwise productivity can appear to decline even if effort per patient increased. Consider methods that adjust for turnover or length-of-stay effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite Work Unit limitation — assumes all occupied bed days are equivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: The Composite Work Unit assumes all occupied bed days are equivalent despite differing patient needs (illness, severity, age, sex, complications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because extra effort per patient may reduce stay length, the C.W.U. can understate effort. Workload measures should account for case mix, severity, and service intensity rather than treating bed days as homogeneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite Work Unit limitation — aggregates different manhour types equally
rubrics_metrics.description: The Composite Work Unit does not differentiate between different types of manhours; a physician, nurse, or ancillary personnel hour are treated equally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One hour of physician time has considerably greater relative value than a similar amount expended by an orderly. Workload/cost measures should avoid aggregating different professional manhours without weighting or separate treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite Work Unit limitation — does not distinguish easy vs hard cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The Composite Work Unit does not make a distinction between an 'easy' case and a 'hard' case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hospitals providing more complex services may be penalized when compared to routine-care hospitals. Measurement systems should include mechanisms to capture complexity/intensity so comparisons are meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of Composite Work Unit — intended purpose matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The Composite Work Unit was developed as a staffing tool; later use as a general resource allocator or funding justification is a different function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a C.W.U. derived for staffing can be used unchanged for funding or trend analysis. If repurposed, adjust base units (and account for cost changes over time) before using for resource allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base-year scaling for trend indices
rubrics_metrics.description: Because 1977 was established as a base year, all input elements are set at 100.000 or 100 percent and each succeeding year's input element is converted to a percentage based on the original year's gross numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When computing trend indices, present items (A),(B),(C) as percentages relative to base year values. Use these percentages (not raw gross numbers) when computing weighted outputs and subsequent productivity indices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Productivity index computation method
rubrics_metrics.description: Productivity per employee (and other indices) is computed by dividing the weighted output (A) by the employee-years (B), both based on their respective percentages rather than gross numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply same percentage-based computation to each index (compensation/employee-years, unit labor cost, etc.). Ensure consistency of base-year conversion across inputs used in index formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain dual datasets for productivity computations
rubrics_metrics.description: DPPO maintains a dual data base of input elements: one 'accepted' set for use by the Bureau of Labor Statistics and an internal set for DPPO's own trend analysis and internal management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a submission-ready standardized dataset and a separate internal dataset for exploratory/management analyses. Be aware that published indices returned by external agencies may reflect different processing choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid presenting purely descriptive analysis when assessing productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: DPPO activities were described as 'heavily skewed toward descriptive rather than analytical topics.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measurement programs should go beyond descriptive reporting to analyze causes and options to change indices (identify drivers, corrective actions), not just present trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate federal medical data into Federal Composite Work Unit
rubrics_metrics.description: Composite Work Unit data from all agencies providing medical services is aggregated into a Federal Composite Work Unit which allows federal medical productivity indices to be computed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aggregating, document scope (which agencies/functions included) and be cautious comparing these aggregated federal indices with private-sector measures due to methodological and conceptual differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid direct comparisons with private-sector indices without adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparing Department of Defense productivity indices with private sector indices has inherent problems stemming from differences in covered activities, measurement methodologies, and measurement concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not directly compare DoD indices with private-sector indices without adjusting for conceptual and methodological differences (scope, output definitions, costing approaches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design requirement — Health Care Unit should be a single number
rubrics_metrics.description: Health Care Unit designers decided that the Health Care Unit: (1) be expressed as a single number;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single-number output measure facilitates aggregation and communication; ensure the single number is interpretable and constructed from well-defined, weighted components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design requirement — Health Care Unit should not be adjusted for facility type
rubrics_metrics.description: Health Care Unit designers decided the HCU should (2) not be adjusted for facility type;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The unit is intended to be applicable across facility types; if facility-specific differences matter, address them through weights or separate performance factors rather than frequent ex-post facility adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design requirement — minimal use of proxies in Health Care Unit
rubrics_metrics.description: Health Care Unit designers decided the HCU should (3) make minimal use of proxies;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor direct measures of treatments/workload from existing accounting and workload records rather than proxy indicators that may distort resource relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design requirement — use existing databases
rubrics_metrics.description: Health Care Unit designers decided the HCU should (4) use existing data bases;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage the Uniform Chart of Accounts and the Medical Expense and Performance Report to minimize additional data collection burden and to maintain compatibility with existing reporting systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design requirement — adaptability and flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Health Care Unit designers decided the HCU should (5) be adaptable and flexible to allow for future changes as required;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a formulation and data sources that allow periodic recalibration of weights and incorporation of new services/technologies with minimal redesign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design requirement — measure quantity not quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Health Care Unit designers decided the HCU should (6) not measure quality of care but rather quantity of care provided;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If quality measurement is desired, deploy separate complementary metrics; do not conflate HCU output counts with quality outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design requirement — usefulness at all organizational levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Health Care Unit designers decided the HCU should (7) be useful at all levels throughout the Organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the metric can be computed and interpreted at unit, facility, service, and DoD-wide levels; document aggregation rules and limits to comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological approach — partition into homogeneous performance factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The general approach: partition the totality of types of care produced into homogeneous categories (Performance Factors); determine the number of 'treatments produced'; take a weighted sum; compute a single number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Uniform Chart of Accounts summary accounts as the set of Performance Factors; ensure categories are defined to capture homogeneous resource consumption patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Uniform Chart of Accounts Performance Factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Uniform Chart of Accounts reports costs and workload data aggregated into inpatient care accounts, ambulatory care accounts, and dental accounts; these 25 Performance Factors were recommended as inputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the UCA summary accounts (the 25 Performance Factors listed) as the basis for performance factor inputs to ensure consistency with accounting and reporting systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health Care Unit formula — HCU = sum(P_i * W_i)
rubrics_metrics.description: HCU = sum over performance factors of P_i * W_i where P_i = the ith performance factor and W_i = the weight factor computed from cost of providing that service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weights should reflect resource consumption so that HCU represents 'one dollar's worth of care' or equivalent resource value; compute HCU consistently across hospitals and services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to weight determination — internal cost data method variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Four internal-cost-based methods considered for weight factor development: (1) use overall average cost per service (DOD-wide), (2) use mean by hospital (average of per-hospital means), (3) mean by hospital adjusted for extremes (discard outliers), (4) median by hospital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each approach yields a candidate weight; consider trade-offs between representativeness and robustness to outliers. The designers later recommended a hospital-mean with outlier removal approach for outpatients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative weight approach — peer groupings
rubrics_metrics.description: Thomas et al. utilized peer groupings for weight factors when designing the system for VA hospitals (place hospitals into groups based on similarity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider clustering hospitals into peer groups and computing group-specific weights when facility heterogeneity is large and renders a single set of weights inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: External data for weights — pros and cons
rubrics_metrics.description: Weights could be developed using civilian (external) data such as CHAMPUS costs, but civilian physician billing practices and geographic cost variation complicate comparability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External data may be useful but be cautious: national, regional, or local civilian costs may not be transferable to military facilities; military salaries are more standardized, so internal data may be preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling duplication between inpatient dispositions and occupied bed days
rubrics_metrics.description: Because inpatient Performance Factors contain dispositions and occupied bed days (both covering the same care), consider: (1) use dispositions only (set OBD weights 0), (2) use occupied bed days only, (3) use direct regression on output (weighted sum of dispositions and OBD), or (4) use indirect regression (convex combinations of methods 1 & 2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate which representation best explains expense variation across hospitals; regression approaches are recommended to derive economically meaningful weights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency and method of updating weights
rubrics_metrics.description: Designers considered continuous, quarterly, annual, base-year, cumulative, or exponential smoothing approaches and recommended recomputing weights at 3 to 5 year intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recompute weights every 3–5 years to balance stability (interpretable trends) and responsiveness (reflect present-level output); no need for continuous updates unless rapid structural changes occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outpatient weight computation recommended method
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended outpatient weight method: for each hospital, compute hospital UCA cost per outpatient performance factor; combine hospitals to compute mean and standard deviation; discard numbers deviating by more than two standard deviations; recompute mean; divide each resulting mean by the fiscal year average cost per disposition to obtain final weights (modified weights relative to inpatient disposition cost).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields a weight reflecting the outpatient visit's value relative to an average inpatient disposition; document outlier rules and base (fiscal year average disposition cost) used for normalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inpatient weight computation — length-of-stay regression
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended inpatient weight method: for each hospital inpatient account compute average length of stay (occupied bed days / dispositions) and cost per disposition; plot LOS vs cost per disposition for each hospital and perform least squares fit. The weight for the inpatient disposition = intercept divided by FY average cost per disposition; the weight for occupied bed day = slope divided by FY average cost per disposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'length of stay regression' yields both disposition and OBD weights grounded in observed cost-length relationships; apply normalization by FY average cost per disposition and document regression diagnostics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use HCU like C.W.U. to derive productivity indices
rubrics_metrics.description: The Health Care Unit can be used in the same manner as the Composite Work Unit for calculating productivity indices (e.g., Health Care Units per physician, per employee, per employee manhours).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once HCU is computed, express productivity metrics by relevant denominators; ensure denominator definitions match those used in prior indices for comparability or document changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight computation — outlier treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: When computing weights from hospital-level costs, numbers which deviate by more than two standard deviations are discarded and a new mean recomputed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply consistent outlier removal rules (e.g., >2 SD) to prevent extreme hospital values from distorting weights; report the number of hospitals excluded and sensitivity to the cutoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalize weights relative to average disposition cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Modified outpatient weights (and inpatient weights after regression) are obtained by dividing by the Fiscal Year average cost per disposition (e.g., $1,129.89 in example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normalization anchors weights to a common monetary baseline so HCU measures are interpretable as relative resource consumption; document the fiscal year and cost base used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability vs accuracy trade-off in weight update frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Designers recommended 3–5 year intervals for recomputing weights to provide stability in interpretation while maintaining accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer intervals improve trend comparability but risk being outdated; choose interval based on observed structural change pace in services, costs, and practice patterns.
